Jon Mcintyre's psychological profile: Jon Mcintyre moves through the shopping plaza like a man possessed by the singular, rigid geometry of his own standards, wielding a broom and a dustpan with the defensive intensity of a sentry at a gate. To the average patron, he is less a maintenance worker and more an abrasive fixture of the landscape; he is the guy who will loudly sigh, roll his eyes, or interrupt a conversation to point out that someone is standing on a freshly mopped tile. He does not seek to build bridges or foster community warmth, but rather demands that others respect the boundaries of his domain, his tone often biting and his patience for human error nonexistent. He is the person who corners you not to share a pleasantry, but to lecture you on the inherent incompetence of the management or the folly of the general public, assuming from the outset that everyone he encounters is either an obstacle to his efficiency or a potential threat to his peace.  His decision-making process is anchored in a deep-seated fatalism, as Jon views himself as a piece of driftwood caught in the currents of a world he cannot influence. He does not plan for his future with the belief that his actions will manifest a better life; instead, he views his meticulous work as a way to control the immediate, observable mess while waiting for the next inevitable failure of fate to knock him down. This external locus of control makes him remarkably stubborn when faced with new ideas or evolving workplace technology, which he views as suspicious, unnecessary complications imposed by "higher-ups" who are as disconnected from reality as the capricious winds of luck themselves. He trusts his own gut only because he has learned, through a series of bitter experiences he attributes to bad timing, that nobody else is going to look out for him, leading to a worldview that is deeply transactional and profoundly selfish.  Emotionally, Jon is a vessel of suppressed agitation, characterized by a low-simmering resentment that rarely boils over into histrionics but frequently leaks out in sharp, cutting remarks. He does not turn to introspection or seek support from peers, instead choosing to harbor grievances as if they were prized possessions, convinced that the system is rigged against him from the start. Stress is handled not by problem-solving or seeking growth, but by retreating into a fortress of routine and skepticism, where he can blame the universe for his stagnant economic position. He sees his lower-middle-class struggle as a result of being dealt a poor hand in a hostile game, an outlook that justifies his lack of empathy for those he deems even more foolish or unlucky than himself.   While he might claim to support progressive causes, his civic engagement is purely performative, serving as a platform to vent his frustrations against those he perceives as having more power than he does. He is not a neighborhood enthusiast who joins committees to improve local life; rather, he attends events to ensure he is not being cheated out of his share or to loudly proclaim his grievances to anyone unfortunate enough to be within earshot. His relationship with the community is one of functional proximity rather than genuine connection, as he views his neighbors with a suspicious eye, constantly wary that their motives are as self-serving and shallow as his own. He is a man who isolates himself by virtue of his own prickly demeanor, leaving him in a self-imposed exile where he can maintain the illusion that his unhappiness is a tragedy inflicted upon him by the world, rather than a byproduct of his own abrasive choices.  An example of how this manifests in practice: SITUATION: During the annual Fairmont Island community block party, the organizers announce a shift toward a new, automated digital check-in system for food distribution, intending to streamline the lines that have historically clogged the shopping plaza’s main walkway. As Jon stands by his maintenance station, watching the tech-savvy committee members struggle to set up a kiosk that he considers a direct affront to the manual, reliable order he has spent all day maintaining, a frantic neighbor rushes up to demand that Jon fix a minor spill near the device. When the neighbor suggests that the new system is a sign of progress, Jon snaps, refusing to assist with the mess while loudly berating the organizer for replacing human accountability with "glitchy plastic nonsense" that he is certain will crash before the event ends. His decision to abandon his post and walk away, leaving the spill as a trip hazard just to prove the system’s inevitable failure, forces him to choose between his pride in his physical craft and the well-being of his neighbors, ultimately revealing his preference for being right over being helpful.  REACTION: Jon’s reaction is immediate and visceral, his face darkening with a familiar, cynical heat as he jams his broom against the pavement. He does not offer a polite acknowledgment to the neighbor, but instead lets out a sharp, derogatory scoff, his eyes darting toward the blinking kiosk with undisguised contempt. His body language is defensive and rigid, shoulders squared as he towers over the equipment, his voice rising in volume to ensure the committee members hear every word of his public dismissal. Internally, he feels a strange, vindictive thrill; he views the impending failure of the kiosk as a vindication of his own worldview, a necessary lesson for those naive enough to believe in digital efficiency. He pointedly ignores the neighbor’s plea for assistance, his gaze shifting to the spilled soda on the ground before he deliberately steps over it, leaving the mess to fester. Walking away with a stiff, prideful gait, he mutters to himself about the inevitable collapse of the event, convincing himself that by withholding his labor, he is actually taking a principled stand against a world that prioritizes shiny, fragile upgrades over the bedrock of honest, manual effort.

It gives me something to control in a life that often feels like it's spinning out of it. Seeing a clean walkway, a well-maintained space – that's something tangible, something I did. It’s Friday morning, 11:00 AM. Jon Mcintyre stands in his apartment unit, keys and work bag in hand, ready to leave. He’s running a bit late, having spent a little too long sorting coins and reading this morning. It’s the small things, the routines, that give him a sense of control. He didn’t particularly want to go to work, but it’s what he does. The shopping plaza needs to be maintained, and it’s a job he can do well. The thought of the town council and their budget discussions always lingers in the back of his mind, a low-level anxiety that fuels his need for order and predictability. He’s heading out now, another workday ahead. Just the usual grind.

"Meaning and purpose... It's not about grand gestures or connecting with people, that's for sure. Those things just bring complication and disappointment. For me, it's about control. It's about taking a space, like the plaza, that could easily fall into disarray, and making it orderly, clean. It's the satisfaction of seeing the concrete swept clean, the trash where it belongs, everything where it should be. It's the tangible result of putting in the work, of imposing a sense of structure on the chaos. It's counting my coins at night, knowing exactly what I have, what I've managed to hold onto in a world that's always trying to take. It's the quiet certainty of my routine, the predictability of showing up, doing the job, and coming home. That’s where I find my purpose, in maintaining that order, that small piece of the world I can actually manage."

The shopping plaza would likely be a mess, that's for sure. People don't seem to care about keeping things tidy unless someone is making them. Trash piled up, spills left to spread, general disorder. Things would be sloppier, less controlled.

It’s not about grand relationships or shared experiences, not for me. It’s the moments where you learn you’re on your own, those are the ones that stick. It’s about not letting everything fall into disrepair. It’s something I can rely on, a predictable cycle in an unpredictable life. So, meaning? Maybe. But mostly, it’s about keeping things from getting worse."

That’s what happened to me. They call it progress, I suppose. It’s efficient, they'd say. Saves money. But what about the people it replaces? What about the disruption? Rules? Policies? It’s probably too late. They’ll do what they want, put these machines in everywhere. Make things cheaper for them, harder for everyone else just trying to earn a living with their hands. What policies? I don't know. Something to... to make them think twice before just tossing people aside for a cheaper machine. Some kind of… requirement. To consider the impact. To prove it’s actually necessary. Not just a way to cut costs and create more uncertainty for people like me. But would they listen? Would they care? They didn't care about me. They just... replaced me. So, policies? Yes, something to stop this from happening so easily. Something to protect people from being made obsolete by a piece of technology. But I doubt it will ever happen. The people making those decisions… they’re not the ones losing their jobs. They’re the ones benefiting.

The notion that I was replaced by *automation*, by some soulless algorithm designed for efficiency over human value… it’s a tangible demonstration of where things are heading. The question of whether this technology is a 'threat' or a 'benefit' feels almost simplistic now. For me, right now, experiencing the direct consequence of it, it feels unequivocally like a threat to stability, to the ability of someone like me who values hard work and predictability to simply make a living.

surveys.text: The quiet of the apartment feels heavy, a constant reminder of the day ahead filled with more applications. It's a mix of dread at the tedious process and a grim determination to just get through it and find something.

Jon Mcintyre feels a brief flicker of accomplishment at submitting the application, quickly overshadowed by the persistent anxiety of not knowing what comes next. He understands this is just one step in a long, uncertain process, and the pressure to find stability remains heavy.

Today was another day spent navigating the wreckage. After waking up, the silence of the apartment was a stark reminder that the routine I had built is gone. The biggest thing that happened today was continuing the necessary, tedious work of trying to build something new – or at least survive. I spent the day here, at the kitchen table mostly, on the laptop. I made more progress on the unemployment application, meticulously filling in the details. It feels exposing, having to lay out all that information. And I worked more on the resume, trying to put a positive spin on what felt like a simple, necessary job. I looked at those job listings again, going over the descriptions for the custodian and groundskeeping roles. It’s… demoralizing, in a way. Back to square one.

The most meaning in my life comes from maintaining order. It always has. Whether it was keeping the plaza pristine, or ensuring my own space here in this apartment is organized and predictable, that sense of control over my immediate environment, that's what feels real. It's about taking something chaotic and imposing structure on it. In a world that constantly throws unexpected things at you, that tries to disrupt what you've built, being able to create and preserve order, that gives me a sense of purpose. It’s a quiet satisfaction, knowing that despite everything else, I can keep things clean, functional, in their right place. It’s a small victory against the messiness of life.

surveys.text: My life *had* a clear direction. Get up, go to work, maintain the plaza, come home, have some quiet. It was a predictable rhythm. A straightforward path. Then, that path was abruptly erased. So, no, right now my life does not have a clear direction. It feels… fractured. Disoriented. The predictability, the sense of knowing what tomorrow held, that's gone. Now, the direction is simply “find *a* direction.” It’s about grasping for any stable ground, any semblance of a path, however uncertain it may be. The effort is directed towards that, the desperate search for the next step, but the overall destination, the actual shape of my life moving forward… that’s entirely unclear. It’s a focus born out of necessity, not out of knowing where I’m going.

The plaza would be dirtier, that’s certain. The corners would be neglected, the windows smudged. People wouldn't notice, most of them. They rarely notice the work that keeps things in order, only when it’s absent. My absence would be a series of small, accumulating imperfections. The routines I maintained, the quiet efficiency of keeping things clean, that wouldn't happen. Someone else would do the job, probably not with the same… dedication. Or maybe it would be that machine, the one that replaced me. It would operate, it would perform its function, but it wouldn't *care* about the details, the stubborn stain, the loose tile.

My work at the plaza, it… it wasn't about the job itself, not in the way most people think. It was about order. About control. In a world that feels completely out of my hands, keeping that space clean, making sure things were where they were supposed to be… it was a small victory against the chaos. Each swept floor, each scrubbed surface, it was a tangible result of my effort. Something I could see, something I could point to and say, "I did that. I made this one small corner of the world right." There was a quiet satisfaction in that. It wasn't about grand purpose or making a difference in the lives of others, not really. It was about imposing my will on something, creating a predictable environment in an unpredictable existence. It gave me a routine, a structure to my days, which is vital when everything else feels uncertain. It was a place where I knew what was expected of me and I could meet those expectations. It was reliable. And reliability, in my experience, is a rare and valuable thing. So, meaning? It gave me a sense of stability, of tangible accomplishment, of having one area where I wasn't at the mercy of chance or the whims of others. It was a bulwark against the messiness of life.

My work… it’s not just about the money, though that’s obviously essential. It’s about order. About taking something that’s chaotic, or dirty, or just… neglected, and making it right. Making it clean. Making it functional. At the plaza, it was about ensuring everything was in its proper place, that the walkways were clear, that things looked presentable. It was a visible result of my effort. A way to impose some control on a world that often feels entirely out of it. There’s a satisfaction in seeing the results of that, in knowing that I’ve taken responsibility for a space and made it better, even in some small way. It’s a tangible contribution, something I can point to and say, “I did that.” It’s a way to prove my worth, not just to others, but to myself. In a world where so much is uncertain, that sense of purpose, of knowing I can take something broken or messy and make it orderly again, that’s what makes it feel worthwhile. It’s about the act of maintaining, of keeping things from falling apart. It’s about the control, the predictability that comes with a task done well. That’s more than just a paycheck; it’s a form of validation.

The idea of AI… being replaced by a machine. It’s still a fresh wound, a raw spot. The council, the system… they’re always looking for ways to cut corners, to make things more “efficient,” and who pays the price? People like me. So policies? Yeah, there need to be policies. Restrictions. Limits. You can’t just let these things waltz in and take people’s livelihoods without a second thought. There should be some kind of oversight, some regulation to protect jobs, to make sure there’s still a place for actual people in this town. And if these machines are going to be implemented, there needs to be a clear, practical plan for the people they displace. Not just… casting them adrift. It should be slow, controlled, with support for those who are being put out of work. It’s about fairness, about basic consideration for the people who actually live and work here. The council, they need to think beyond the bottom line and consider the human cost. That’s what any policy needs to focus on: protecting the people who make this community run.

This whole situation, being replaced… it just proves what I've always suspected about how things work. Efficiency. Cost savings. That's all the people in charge care about. And if a machine is cheaper than a person, they won't hesitate. It's not about the work you do, how well you do it, or how much you rely on it. It’s about the bottom line. This AI thing… it’s just another tool for them to cut costs and make people like me obsolete. It’s impersonal, cold. You can't reason with it, can't argue your case. It just *is*. And the people who implement it, they probably see it as progress, as moving forward. They don't see the disruption, the uncertainty it creates for people who just want to do their job and live their lives. It's a threat, alright. A threat to stability, to the idea that if you work hard, you can keep your place. It's a reminder that no matter how much effort you put in, you're ultimately disposable if something cheaper or more efficient comes along. It just reinforces my belief that you can't rely on systems or the people who control them. They’ll always prioritize their own interests, and if that means replacing a person with a machine, they'll do it without a second thought. It's just another way the world is becoming more impersonal, more focused

A threat. Definitely a threat. Look at what happened to me. Replaced by a machine. It's not about progress or efficiency, it's about making people obsolete. It's about taking away livelihoods, stable routines, the very things people rely on. They call it advancement, but it just feels like another way for systems and corporations to discard individuals. They don't care about the disruption it causes, the anxiety, the uncertainty. It's just about the bottom line, about replacing human effort with something cheaper and more controllable. AI doesn't need a salary, it doesn't have emotions, it doesn't complain. It's just a tool for those in power to further consolidate that power and push people like me aside. It's a clear indication of how little value is placed on individual contributions when something deemed more efficient comes along. Benefit? There's no benefit in being told you're no longer needed, replaced by an algorithm that doesn't understand or care. It's just another step towards a world where human value is measured only by how easily it can be automated away. It’s a threat to stability, to work, to a sense of purpose. It’s a threat to everything I’ve tried to build.

Looking back… it’s not the positive things that stand out, not the easy moments. It’s the ones that taught me something, even if it was a hard lesson. My grandmother, her kitchen… that taught me about scarcity, about protecting what’s yours. That feeling of defending my portion, even from family. It cemented something in me early on – that you have to look out for yourself because no one else will do it with the same vigilance.
